newsitem.title: USA: TENNIS-RUSEDSKI QUITS WITH BAD WRIST AGAINST SAMPRAS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-RUSEDSKI QUITS WITH BAD WRIST AGAINST SAMPRAS.

text.p: Briton Greg
Rusedski's dream of knocking-off America's three top players
in consecutive matches ended Sunday when he retired in tears
with a wrist injury in the final of the Sybase Open tennis
tournament.
Rusedski, who had been icing his sore wrist all week,
retired at 6-3 0-5 against top-seed Pete Sampras and blamed
tennis officials for his injury which he said occurred because
they used different weights of balls in tournaments.
Rusedski, the seventh seed, said his wrist began hurting
him Sunday morning and gradually got worse during the match.
While attempting a forehand passing shot at down 0-40, 0-3 in
the second set, Rusedski grimaced in pain as his racket flew
out of his hand.
Sampras would hold at love the next game to go up 5-0.
Rusedski, down 0-30 on his serve, walked up the net and
called it quits. He then broke down crying.
"If I'm not 100 percent that's no point in continuing,"
Rusedski said. "It's no good to continue to play and lose 6-0,
6-0. There's no value to the crowd or my wrist."
An ATP official said Rusedski has sustained a strained
ligament in wrist. He will see a specialist in Los Angeles on
Monday, but is not concerned that he could be in for
career-threatening wrist surgery.
After the match, Rusedski lashed out at the ATP Tour for
not standardising ball weights at various tournaments.
"You play one week with a Slazenger which is soft, you
play with a ATP Tour ball, then you play with a hard Wilson
ball," Rusedski said. "They got to do something about this
because it's causing players arm and wrist problems. They've
got to make some sense out of this and standardise one single
ball."
Sampras disagreed.
"I think the tournaments do a good job with the balls,"
Sampras said. "I haven't had any arm problems in two years.
The only time I've complained was at the Australian, when the
balls were soft and flat.
"I think Greg's problem is that serving at 139 mph (223.6
kph) can't be good for your arm. He serves so hard with so
much wrist that it's not surprising he had a problem."
A number of tennis observers believe that light rackets
are a contributing factor to arm injuries. While Sampras is
capable of hitting a serve 132 mph (212.4), he most keeps his
serves in the 120s (193s) and uses a 385-gram racket,
significantly heavier than Rusedski's 365-gram frame.
Rusedski has been all but unstoppable on serve this year,
holding serve in 87 consecutive games entering his match with
Sampras. He had crushed 55 aces in four matches before facing
Sampras, keying his upset victories of number-two seed Chang
and number three Agassi.
The one-time Canadian citizen continued his blaze of glory
in the first set, slamming four straight aces in third game,
two of which registered over 130 mph (209 kph)
Ahead 4-3, Rusedski showed off his improved groundstrokes
by breaking Sampras with a running forehand down the line to
go up 4-3. Rusedski would knock off three service winners in
the next game to take the set 6-3.
"Greg was phenomenal," said Sampras, who became the first
player to repeat as the Sybase titlist since John McEnroe in
1978-'79. "He only missed four serves in the first set.
"At the end of the first set, I had pretty much accepted
that if he was going to keep playing like that, he was too
good."
Sampras regained his composure in the second set, breaking
Rusedski in the second game with a picture-perfect backhand
down the line, stopping Rusedski's streak of consecutive games
holding serve at 92.
Rusedski said that by that point, he was finished.
"My kick serve was pretty useless because I couldn't get
around or over it, and I couldn't hit a forehand," Rusedski
said. "When you're playing Sampras and you can't hit your best
serve or your forehand, it's kind of hard to win."
A disappointed Rusedski will likely drop out of the
tournament in Memphis this week and lamented his lost chance
against the world number one.
"I had a good opportunity to win the match today but
Pete's a great player and we won't know [who would have won]
until we play the next time."
